requirements.text: An automated method of asset discovery is used at least fortnightly to support the detection of assets for subsequent vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: Live demo of the discovery method plus dated scan records, gap never exceeding 14 days, scope covering known assets; unknown assets surfaced between scans must show evidence of investigation.
requirements.why: A fortnightly Actions cron enumerating Vercel projects/deployments/functions, Supabase projects and buckets, plus an SBOM of the dependency trees, committed as a dated manifest. Analogue because ASD's control is DISCOVERY of unknown assets and a manifest built from committed declarations cannot surface an undeclared one.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner with an up-to-date vulnerability database is used for vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.measurable: Demo of a scan plus the timestamp of the scanner's last database update; ASD expects ideally within 24 hours of the scan.
requirements.why: osv-scanner, Trivy and pnpm audit query a live advisory database at invocation, so currency is structural.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The scheduled workflow job log recording scanner version and advisory-database pull timestamp alongside the scan timestamp, plus the SARIF artefact uploaded to GitHub code scanning.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least daily to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in online services.
requirements.timeframes: At least daily
requirements.measurable: Dated scan records with no gap exceeding 24 hours, plus reconciliation of scanned online services against the online services known to be in use.
requirements.why: ASD's FAQ defines an online service as any service directly accessible over the internet, expressly including a cloud service. The deployed Next.js app, its route handlers and Server Actions, and the Supabase PostgREST/GoTrue/Realtime/Storage endpoints all qualify.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A daily-cron workflow running osv-scanner over pnpm-lock.yaml plus a ZAP baseline / testssl.sh scan against the production URL; run history is the cadence evidence, a committed route inventory the scope evidence.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least weekly to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, and security products.
requirements.timeframes: At least weekly
requirements.measurable: Dated scan records with no gap exceeding 7 days and confirmation the scanned list includes every office suite, browser, extension, email client, PDF reader and security product in scope.
requirements.why: Reachable slice is the app's own content-handling client dependencies — pdf.js/react-native-pdf, react-native-webview, DOMPurify, the Markdown/HTML pipeline, image and font decoders, browserslist targets — scanned weekly by a scoped osv-scanner job. That is the in-app analogue of the class ASD singles out because it parses attacker-supplied content.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Office productivity suites, email clients and endpoint security products on staff workstations.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least fortnightly to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, and security products.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: Dated scan records no more than 14 days apart with scope extending to every remaining application, not only the commonly-targeted classes.
requirements.why: The catch-all class here is the rest of the dependency graph: remaining runtime and transitive packages, devDependencies, build tooling, Expo native modules, Edge Function Deno imports, container base images and pinned Actions.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A scheduled (daily, over-satisfying the floor) osv-scanner/Trivy run over pnpm-lock.yaml, supabase/functions deno.lock and .github/workflows action pins, with SARIF uploaded to code scanning.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in online services are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: Online service versions and install dates reviewed against vendor patch release dates to confirm 48 hours or less; criticality and exploit existence from CISA KEV, SANS ISC or MSRC. ASD warns a scanner may not detect missing non-patch vendor mitigations such as configuration changes. Trigger is disjunctive: vendor-critical OR a working exploit exists.
requirements.why: Elapsed time between advisory publication and the production deployment SHA carrying the fix is exactly computable from advisory metadata, the lockfile diff and the deployment record. The 'other vendor mitigations' limb is satisfiable in-repo by a middleware block or feature flag ahead of the patch.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A CI gate failing the build on any critical or KEV-listed advisory in a production dependency, plus Dependabot security updates with auto-merge on green; evidence is advisory publish timestamp versus the Vercel production deployment timestamp for the bump commit.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in online services are applied within two weeks of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: Two weeks
requirements.measurable: Same evidence chain as PA-06 with a 14-day window for vendor-rated non-critical vulnerabilities with no working exploit.
requirements.why: Identical mechanism on a 14-day budget; advisory date versus the production deploy carrying the bump, both timestamped.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A CI check failing when any open non-critical advisory against a production dependency exceeds 14 days since publication, plus a Renovate/Dependabot cadence with a recorded merge-by SLA.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, and security products are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.supersedes: The ML1/ML2 flat two-week rule for this class.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: Installed application inventory with versions and install dates reviewed against vendor release dates, applying 48 hours where vendor-critical or a working exploit exists.
requirements.why: The same 48-hour window applied to the shipped content-handling client surface, plus the Expo OTA channel — the only mechanism in this stack that can push a fix to installed mobile clients inside 48 hours without App Store review. Measurable as advisory timestamp versus EAS Update publish timestamp.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The office suite, email client and endpoint security product on staff workstations.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, and security products are applied within two weeks of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.supersedes: The ML1/ML2 flat two-week rule for this class.
requirements.timeframes: Two weeks
requirements.measurable: Same inventory-versus-release-date method against 14 days where the vendor rated the vulnerability non-critical and no working exploit exists.
requirements.why: Non-critical advisories against shipped content-rendering dependencies reaching production web and a published Expo update within two weeks. Textually new at ML3 but not a tightening — ML1/ML2 already required two weeks for this class unconditionally.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The office suite, email client and endpoint security product on staff workstations.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, and security products are applied within one month of release.
requirements.timeframes: One month
requirements.measurable: Full application inventory reviewed against vendor release dates confirming nothing is more than a month behind. This bullet carries NO criticality or exploit qualifier at any level — one month applies unconditionally, even to a critical vulnerability with a working exploit.
requirements.why: The most directly automatable requirement in the framework for a repository: for every advisory affecting a lockfile package, compare its publication date to the commit that bumped it.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A CI check failing the build when the gap between any advisory publication date and the corresponding lockfile bump exceeds 30 days, plus renovate.json encoding a monthly-at-worst merge SLA.

requirements.text: Online services that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.
requirements.measurable: Demonstration of online service versions in use checked against vendor supported-version lists, or a scanner assessing end-of-life status.
requirements.why: Concrete and in-repo: a Node runtime past EOL, a Next.js major outside its support window, a Supabase Postgres major past community EOL, a deprecated Vercel runtime, or an abandoned package serving a production endpoint. Remediation is a version bump plus migration.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A CI check querying the endoflife.date API for every runtime and framework major declared in package.json engines, .nvmrc, vercel.json and supabase/config.toml, failing on any past EOL. NOTE: overlaps POS-16 — count this artefact once, not in both strategies.

requirements.text: Office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, Adobe Flash Player, and security products that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.
requirements.measurable: Versions in use checked against vendor supported lists. ASD directs assessors to check hotfix KB4577586 as evidence Adobe Flash Player was removed, with the caveat it only removes Flash installed by Microsoft Windows.
requirements.why: Removing archived or deprecated content-handling packages from package.json and dropping vendor-unsupported browsers from browserslist — both diffable and enforceable by a CI check on npm deprecation flags and browserslist EOL targets.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Nothing in a repository removes Adobe Flash Player, an EOL Office install, or an unsupported browser from a staff laptop. ASD still names Flash despite EOL in December 2020.

requirements.text: Applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, Adobe Flash Player, and security products that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.
requirements.measurable: ASD directs assessors to use the ML1 method and extend it to ALL applications — no unsupported application present anywhere. This is the quiet bullet that turns 'no dead browsers or Office installs' into 'no unsupported software anywhere on the system'.
requirements.why: Extended to all applications this is 'no unmaintained dependency anywhere in the tree', literally satisfiable and provable; removal is a lockfile change.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A CI check failing on any npm registry deprecation flag in pnpm-lock.yaml, any Expo SDK below Expo's supported matrix, any Deno std past its support line, or any pinned GitHub Action from an archived repository.

requirements.text: An automated method of asset discovery is used at least fortnightly to support the detection of assets for subsequent vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: Demo of the discovery method identifying workstations, servers and network devices plus dated records no more than 14 days apart; unknown assets found between scans must be immediately investigated and treated as suspicious until confirmed.
requirements.why: A fortnightly cron enumerating base images and runtimes pinned in Dockerfile, .nvmrc, package.json engines, supabase/config.toml and runs-on declarations, committed as a dated manifest. Analogue on both counts: wrong asset class, and declarations cannot discover the undeclared.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The organisation's workstation, server and network device estate.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner with an up-to-date vulnerability database is used for vulnerability scanning activities.
requirements.measurable: Live demo of a scan plus evidence of when the scanner's database was last updated, ideally within 24 hours.
requirements.why: A Trivy or Grype step refreshing its CVE database on every run satisfies this literally; a stale offline database would be visible as a failure.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The scheduled workflow log recording the Trivy/Grype version and its vulnerability-DB download timestamp immediately preceding the scan.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least daily to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in operating systems of internet-facing servers and internet-facing network devices.
requirements.timeframes: At least daily
requirements.measurable: Demo of a scan plus dated records covering every internet-facing server and network device, no more than 24 hours apart.
requirements.why: No network devices exist here and the host OS is vendor-managed. Reachable slice: a daily scan of the internet-facing runtime layer the repo pins — Node version for route handlers, Deno version for Edge Functions, any Docker base image, and the Supabase Postgres platform version.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Operating systems of any servers or network devices the organisation operates; the managed host OS the tenant cannot scan.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least fortnightly to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: Demo of a scan plus dated records covering workstations, non-internet-facing servers and network devices, no more than 14 days apart.
requirements.why: The repo declares scannable non-internet-facing compute: the CI runner image pinned in .github/workflows, the devcontainer/Docker base image, and the local Supabase container images pinned in supabase/config.toml.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Developer and staff workstations — the majority of this requirement's scope — need MDM and an endpoint vulnerability scanner.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least fortnightly to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in drivers.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: ASD: apply the ML1 scanning method to drivers. Dated records whose scope demonstrably includes device drivers, no more than 14 days apart.
requirements.why: Drivers exist only on physical hardware. Expo native modules and React Native native code are application libraries and fall under Patch applications; treating them as drivers would be inflation.

requirements.text: A vulnerability scanner is used at least fortnightly to identify missing patches or updates for vulnerabilities in firmware.
requirements.timeframes: At least fortnightly
requirements.measurable: ASD: apply the ML1 scanning method to firmware. Dated records covering BIOS/UEFI, NIC and network device firmware, no more than 14 days apart.
requirements.why: Under Vercel and Supabase the hardware and its firmware are the provider's responsibility and invisible to the tenant; the mobile app cannot see handset firmware.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of internet-facing servers and internet-facing network devices are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: Scanner output listing operating systems, versions and install dates cross-referenced against vendor release dates. ASD warns WSUS reports patches as deployed without confirming successful application or reboot.
requirements.why: The OS is vendor-managed but version selection lives in the repo: a commit bumping .nvmrc / engines.node / vercel.json nodeVersion / the Dockerfile base tag plus a Supabase platform upgrade, then redeploy. A daily critical-CVE gate enforces the clock; advisory-versus-deployment timestamps are the evidence.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Kernel and OS packages of the managed host, patchable only by Vercel and Supabase, and any servers or network devices the organisation runs.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of internet-facing servers and internet-facing network devices are applied within two weeks of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: Two weeks
requirements.measurable: Same scanner-versus-release-date comparison showing 14 days or less, plus the basis on which non-critical and no-working-exploit was determined.
requirements.why: Identical mechanism on a 14-day service level: a CI policy failing when a non-critical advisory affecting the pinned runtime, base image tag or Postgres major has been open more than 14 days without a bump.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The managed host OS and any organisation-operated servers or network devices.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.supersedes: The ML1/ML2 unqualified one-month rule for this class.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 method but apply 48 hours where vendor-critical or a working exploit exists; scanner output or hotfix listings showing 48 hours or less between release and successful application.
requirements.why: Repo-satisfiable slice is the declared non-internet-facing compute — CI runner image pins, devcontainer base, local Supabase container tags — bumpable within 48 hours by a scheduled job that opens a blocking PR and fails the pipeline until merged.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The developer and staff workstation fleet, the dominant asset class here; a real ML3 assessment fails on that limb alone.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.supersedes: The ML1/ML2 unqualified one-month rule for this class.
requirements.timeframes: One month
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 method where vulnerabilities are non-critical and no working exploit exists; evidence showing one month or less between release and successful application.
requirements.why: A scheduled freshness job comparing pinned digests for the CI runner image, devcontainer base and local Supabase container tags against vendor release dates, failing if any pin lags a non-critical advisory by more than 30 days.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The developer and staff workstation fleet.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in drivers are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: A driver inventory with installed versions and install dates compared against vendor driver release dates for vendor-critical or actively exploited driver vulnerabilities.
requirements.why: Driver patching happens on physical machines the organisation owns; the repo ships no drivers and the cloud application runs on hardware whose drivers are the provider's.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in drivers are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: One month
requirements.measurable: Driver inventory showing versions and install dates within one month of vendor release. Note the window is one month, not two weeks — drivers and firmware get a more lenient non-critical window than internet-facing operating systems.
requirements.why: Driver currency is purely a property of the organisation's physical endpoint estate.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in firmware are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: 48 hours
requirements.measurable: Firmware inventory (BIOS/UEFI, network device and peripheral firmware) with versions and update dates compared against vendor firmware release dates.
requirements.why: Firmware updating is a physical-estate operation; in a managed deployment the tenant cannot see, let alone update, host firmware.

requirements.text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in firmware are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
requirements.timeframes: One month
requirements.measurable: Firmware inventory showing versions updated within one month of vendor release for non-critical, no-known-exploit vulnerabilities.
requirements.why: Firmware currency belongs to the organisation's hardware estate and its vendor relationships.

requirements.text: The latest release, or the previous release, of operating systems are used.
requirements.measurable: Scanner output listing operating systems and versions checked against latest vendor versions, or 'winver' for Windows and 'cat /etc/os-release' for Linux across workstations and servers. Every in-scope OS must be on the current release or the one immediately preceding it.
requirements.why: DOWNGRADED from the source research's 'direct'. The subject is the operating systems of the organisation's workstations, servers and network devices. android.targetSdkVersion and ios.deploymentTarget are what the app TARGETS on other people's handsets — a repo cannot put a customer's phone on the current iOS major — and runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 is a build host. Honest analogue: a CI rule asserting every OS-release pin the repo does own is current or one behind.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The operating systems of the organisation's workstations, servers and network devices — the actual subject of the requirement.

requirements.text: Operating systems that are no longer supported by vendors are replaced.
requirements.measurable: Scanner output or 'winver'/'cat /etc/os-release' checked against vendors' supported lists; any unsupported OS must be shown to have been REPLACED, not risk-accepted. ASD's verb here is 'replaced', versus 'removed' in Patch applications.
requirements.why: DOWNGRADED from 'direct'. A Node runtime and a Postgres major are not operating systems, and claiming them here double-counts evidence already claimed at PA-11. The genuine analogue is CI checking the OS releases the repo does pin — container base image, CI runner image, minimum supported iOS/Android OS — against vendor EOL.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Operating systems of workstations, servers and network devices; the managed host OS.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users to their organisation’s online services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive data.
requirements.measurable: Assessor attempts to log on to the organisation's own online services; two or more factors should be requested, possibly sequentially. The assessor must also probe for additional internet-exposed authentication portals the organisation did not disclose.
requirements.why: The deployed Next.js/Expo + Supabase application IS an organisation-operated online service, and enforcement is server-side and testable rather than a client gate.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A migration whose RLS policies on sensitive tables include the predicate (auth.jwt()->>'aal') = 'aal2', plus an integration test authenticating password-only and asserting an empty result set / 401; plus a committed inventory of every auth entry point (web route handlers, Expo deep links, tRPC procedures, Edge Functions) answering ASD's undisclosed-portal probe.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users to third-party online services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive data.
requirements.measurable: Assessor attempts to log on to the third-party online services staff use; vendor non-support is the only accepted excuse for absence.
requirements.why: A committed provider register (GitHub org, Vercel team, Supabase org, Expo/EAS, Sentry, any provider in the env schema) with an mfa_enforced column and an owner, plus a CI assertion where an API exposes it — gh api /orgs/{org} --jq .two_factor_requirement_enabled must be true.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Actual MFA enforcement in each vendor's admin console.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication (where available) is used to authenticate users to third-party online services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s non-sensitive data.
requirements.measurable: Same as MFA-02; '(where available)' means availability, not convenience, is the test.
requirements.why: Same register mechanism extended to the lower-sensitivity vendor tail, with a CI check failing when a row reads available: true, enforced: false.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Enforcement in each vendor console.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users to their organisation’s online customer services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive customer data.
requirements.measurable: Assessor attempts to log on to the organisation's own online customer services as a STAFF user, not a customer.
requirements.why: This is the staff/back-office side of the deployed application — the admin console or support-agent view through which employees touch customer records.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: RLS policies on customer-data tables requiring both an is_staff claim and (auth.jwt()->>'aal') = 'aal2', shipped as a migration, plus a test asserting a staff JWT at aal1 returns zero rows.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users to third-party online customer services that process, store or communicate their organisation’s sensitive customer data.
requirements.measurable: Assessor attempts to log on to third-party online customer services staff access — an outsourced CRM, help desk or identity portal holding customer data.
requirements.why: The repo declares which processors touch customer data via env schemas and SDK imports; a committed data-processor register keyed off those imports with an MFA-enforcement column, plus a CI grep failing when a new customer-data SDK is imported without a register row.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The vendor-side MFA toggle on each processor account.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate customers to online customer services that process, store or communicate sensitive customer data.
requirements.measurable: Assessor logs on as a customer and specifically discusses whether MFA is part of account creation or an after-the-fact opt-in — the November 2023 change removed easy customer opt-out, so opt-in-only is a fail.
requirements.why: The end users of the generated app ARE the customers; this is the most repo-provable authentication row in the framework.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The signup state machine making factor enrolment a required step rather than a settings toggle; an RLS predicate requiring aal2 on sensitive customer tables; an E2E test asserting a fresh account cannot reach data screens without enrolling; and a scheduled query asserting the count of AAL1-capable accounts holding sensitive data is zero.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate privileged users of systems.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes a privileged user authenticating to a workstation, and separately to a server, checking multiple factors are requested.
requirements.why: 'Systems' means workstations and servers. The server limb has a cloud referent: MFA required on Vercel owner and Supabase project admin accounts, no long-lived service-role keys in developer hands (CI-only, OIDC-federated), MFA-backed required-reviewer approval for production deploys and migrations, and the app's admin role gated at aal2 in middleware and RLS.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Workstation OS logon by privileged users — an endpoint/IdP control (Windows Hello for Business, smart cards, Conditional Access).

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate unprivileged users of systems.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes an unprivileged user authenticating to a workstation and checks multiple factors are requested.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED for consistency: the source marked MFA-07 analogue and MFA-08 org-only on the identical noun 'systems', justified only by bookkeeping. If 'systems' stretches to the Supabase/Vercel project for privileged users it stretches for unprivileged ones — read-only Supabase members, Vercel viewer-role staff, support accounts — with MFA enforceable and evidenced from the org member list. The app's own end-user MFA is NOT claimed here; it is claimed at MFA-01/04/06.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Workstation OS logon by ordinary staff — the dominant limb, entirely an endpoint/IdP concern.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication is used to authenticate users of data repositories.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests a list of ALL data repositories for the system plus screenshots of a user attempting to access each, showing multiple factors. ASD defines a data repository as 'a location in which data is stored, managed and made available to users' — file shares, databases, object stores, not just the primary database.
requirements.why: The repository inventory is enumerable from the repo (Postgres via supabase/migrations, Storage buckets via bucket declarations). Application paths can require aal2 in RLS including on storage.objects, and a CI grep can fail on any RLS policy over a sensitive table or bucket lacking the AAL2 predicate. Analogue because human console access is a platform-account property.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: MFA on Supabase dashboard/SQL editor accounts and any direct psql path.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication uses either: something users have and something users know, or something users have that is unlocked by something users know or are.
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses the implementation for users and customers, distinguishing multi-step from multi-factor and ranking strength (security key / smart card / passkey > hardware OTP > OTP app > push or SMS). Per the FAQ, security questions are NOT a valid memorised secret and biometrics are never a primary factor.
requirements.why: Which factor combinations the application accepts is entirely a property of its auth configuration and code.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: supabase/config.toml committed with only ASD-valid factor types enabled (TOTP + password, or WebAuthn) and Phone/SMS disabled; a test asserting enrolment of a disallowed factor type is rejected; a test asserting no 'remember this device' cookie path can downgrade a later session to one factor (ASD rules this out and requires MFA for re-authentication); and a grep asserting no security-question recovery path exists.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication used for authenticating users of online services is phishing-resistant.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes unprivileged and privileged users authenticating to the organisation's own AND third-party online services, checking a phishing-resistant form is required. ASD's exemplars are security keys, smart cards and passkeys; TOTP apps, push notifications and SMS/voice are explicitly NOT phishing-resistant.
requirements.why: DOWNGRADED from 'direct'. The requirement spans the organisation's own AND third-party online services; scoring it direct on one limb is inflation. The app's own limb is real and testable — WebAuthn/FIDO2 only, RP ID and origins pinned to production hostnames, TOTP enrolment refused — but the third-party limb degrades to the register approach of MFA-02.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Phishing-resistant MFA on every third-party online service staff use.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication used for authenticating customers of online customer services is phishing-resistant.
requirements.supersedes: The ML2 requirement that a phishing-resistant OPTION be provided.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes a customer authenticating and checks a phishing-resistant form is REQUIRED, not merely offered. An implementation letting customers pick SMS fails.
requirements.why: Passkeys are first-class on both targets — WebAuthn in the browser for Next.js, platform passkeys via the iOS/Android credential managers for Expo, whose association files are committed to the repo and served by the deployed app.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: public/.well-known/apple-app-site-association and public/.well-known/assetlinks.json served with correct content type; supabase/config.toml with only the WebAuthn factor enabled; an E2E test asserting an account without a passkey cannot reach sensitive screens; a scheduled query asserting zero customer accounts hold a non-phishing-resistant factor; and a test that no emailed-magic-link or SMS-reset recovery path reintroduces a phishable route.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication used for authenticating users of systems is phishing-resistant.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes unprivileged and privileged users authenticating to a workstation, and a privileged user to a server, checking a security key, smart card or passkey is required. ASD's change notes cite smart cards, security keys or Windows Hello for Business for workstations.
requirements.why: Splits like MFA-07. Reachable: Vercel, Supabase and GitHub organisation accounts restricted to WebAuthn/passkey or SSO with a phishing-resistant IdP, GitHub org set to require 2FA, and no long-lived service-role or deploy token bypassing the human factor. Machine-checkable slice: OIDC federation rather than static secrets in the workflow YAML, required environment reviewers, and secret scanning failing on a committed service-role key.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Workstation OS logon for both privileged and unprivileged users.

requirements.text: Multi-factor authentication used for authenticating users of data repositories is phishing-resistant.
requirements.measurable: Assessor observes unprivileged and privileged users authenticating to each repository in the MFA-09 inventory and checks a phishing-resistant form is required.
requirements.why: The application path can go beyond AAL2: Supabase exposes the authentication method reference in the JWT, so an RLS predicate can require both aal2 and a WebAuthn AMR entry, refusing a TOTP-only session at the database. Analogue because the human console path is a platform setting, and because Supabase WebAuthn factor support is newer than TOTP and must be verified on the actual project before claiming this.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Passkey/security-key enforcement on Supabase dashboard, SQL editor and direct psql access.

requirements.text: Successful and unsuccessful multi-factor authentication events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: For Windows estates, RSoP showing Audit Logon and Audit Special Logon set to 'Success and Failure' with central storage. ASD explicitly allows that for certain MFA implementations this guidance is not applicable, in which case the assessor discusses whether logging exists for all systems users authenticate to. Both successful AND unsuccessful — success-only logging fails.
requirements.why: This is the 'certain MFA implementations' escape ASD wrote into the guidance; Supabase Auth emits entries for login, factor challenge and factor verification including failures.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A committed log-drain configuration shipping Supabase Auth logs to a central sink, or a migration creating an auth_audit table written by a trigger/Edge Function; plus an integration test performing one successful and one deliberately failed MFA challenge and asserting two distinguishable rows land in the sink. The failure mode to test for is logging login and dropping the failed-challenge event.

requirements.text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether a SIEM, or equivalent, protects logs from unauthorised modification and deletion; demonstrable write-once retention is markedly stronger than assertion.
requirements.why: No endpoint specificity, and append-only logging is a schema property reviewable in the diff and provable by a negative test. The one shared-spine clause a repository can prove outright.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A migration creating the audit table with RLS granting INSERT and SELECT only and no UPDATE/DELETE policy for any role including service_role; REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE from all application roles; a trigger raising on mutation; a committed test attempting UPDATE and DELETE as every role and asserting both refused; a CI check that no later migration re-grants those privileges; and a one-way drain to an object-lock/WORM sink the app's credentials cannot delete from. ONE artefact — counted once across MFA-16, RAP-22, AC-12, UAH-20.

requirements.text: Event logs from internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise; supporting evidence is detection rules plus records of alerts having been triaged.
requirements.why: CANONICAL for this clause in all four strategies. Vercel functions and Supabase Edge Functions ARE internet-facing servers so the log source is in scope, and detection-as-code is committable (auth-failure spikes, RLS-denial bursts, CSP violation floods, anomalous privileged-procedure calls, each with severity and routing, plus a synthetic-event test firing a real alert in CI). Analogue because ASD's verb is 'are analysed' and timely triage is staffed.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Human triage of the alerts and the triage records the assessor examines.

requirements.text: Event logs from non-internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor non-internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise; the ML3 extension is coverage beyond internet-facing infrastructure.
requirements.why: CANONICAL. The nearest true referent is the managed Postgres instance (genuinely non-internet-reachable once network restrictions are on) plus CI runners and scheduled workers. Committable: pgaudit and log-drain settings as configuration, alert rules for direct connections outside expected ranges, service-role queries outside migration windows, unexpected DDL, lockfile mutation during a build, workflow self-modification, deploys from unexpected actors.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Any internal server estate the organisation operates; human triage.

requirements.text: Event logs from workstations are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor workstation event logs for signs of compromise, requiring central collection rather than local retention.
requirements.why: CANONICAL. Workstation telemetry means EDR/Sysmon/Windows Security streams from staff endpoints. Mapping this onto Expo client telemetry is a category error — the mobile app runs on customers' personal devices. Mapping it onto CI runner logs would double-count the RAP-08 Secure Admin Workstation analogue.

requirements.text: Cyber security events are analysed in a timely manner to identify cyber security incidents.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses how SOC analysts analyse events to determine whether an incident occurred; the incident register also evidences this analysis.
requirements.why: CANONICAL (the source split this org-only twice, analogue twice, on identical text). This is the human escalation judgement, evidenced by an incident register. The detection rules feeding it are already claimed at the two log-analysis rows.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to the chief information security officer, or one of their delegates, as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to the CISO or delegate and judges whether typical timeframes are reasonable; evidence is discovery-to-notification intervals in the incident register.
requirements.why: Internal escalation to a named organisational officer, presupposing an org chart and a reporting relationship. Routing an alert to a distribution list is not the reporting obligation.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to ASD as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to ASD and whether timeframes are reasonable; corroborating evidence is ReportCyber submissions or ASD case references in the incident register.
requirements.why: External regulatory notification by a legal entity to a national authority. No repository has standing to report or any artefact evidencing it.

requirements.text: Following the identification of a cyber security incident, the cyber security incident response plan is enacted.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests the incident response plan and discusses the extent to which it is followed after an incident; post-incident reviews are the strongest evidence.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — DOWNGRADED from the source's lone 'analogue' against three org-only calls on identical text. A repo can host the plan and automate response steps (session revocation, key rotation, kill-switch flag), but the requirement is that the plan IS ENACTED after an identified incident, assessed by discussing real past incidents.

requirements.text: Requests for privileged access to systems, applications and data repositories are validated when first requested.
requirements.measurable: For every active privileged grant, a dated validation/approval record predating or coinciding with the grant, naming the business need and approving authority.
requirements.why: Hold the privileged-access roster in the repo (CODEOWNERS plus a checked-in access manifest) and grant the app's admin role only via reviewed migration or an approval-carrying RPC, making git history the validation record. Grants made ad hoc in the Supabase or Vercel console leave no such record and fail.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Approval authority and business-need judgement for platform-console grants.

requirements.text: Privileged access to systems, applications and data repositories is disabled after 12 months unless revalidated.
requirements.timeframes: 12 months
requirements.measurable: No privileged grant has an unrevalidated age greater than 12 months; evidence is a dated revalidation register or an automated expiry mechanism plus its execution log.
requirements.why: Literally implementable in the application and CI, with machine-checkable rows and job logs rather than a hand-maintained register.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A migration adding granted_at/expires_at to the privileged-role table with an RLS predicate that stops honouring the admin role past expiry; a pg_cron or Edge Function job revoking at the 12-month boundary; and a CI cron diffing the live GitHub org admin list and Supabase member list against a dated in-repo roster, failing on any grant older than 12 months without recorded revalidation.

requirements.text: Privileged access to systems and applications is disabled after 45 days of inactivity.
requirements.timeframes: 45 days
requirements.measurable: Last-use timestamps per privileged account with no enabled account exceeding 45 days since last use; evidence is the disablement job log plus a query over last-activity data.
requirements.why: Supabase exposes auth.users.last_sign_in_at, the app can record last_privileged_action_at, and GitHub's API reports token and deploy-key last-used dates, so machine identities are covered too.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A scheduled job (pg_cron or Actions cron) disabling the privileged role at 45 days of inactivity and revoking idle privileged tokens, with its run log plus a committed test asserting a 46-day-idle admin row no longer satisfies the RLS admin predicate.

requirements.text: Privileged users are assigned a dedicated privileged user account to be used solely for duties requiring privileged access.
requirements.measurable: Each privileged user has a separate attributable privileged account distinct from their day-to-day account, with audit logs showing privileged operations only ever under the privileged account.
requirements.why: Admin capability is never a flag on a person's everyday application account — privileged identity is a distinct principal or an explicitly assumed, session-recorded role; and CI authenticates as a dedicated machine identity via GitHub OIDC rather than a maintainer's PAT.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Separate privileged accounts in the organisation's identity provider for platform-console access.

requirements.text: Privileged access to systems, applications and data repositories is limited to only what is required for users and services to undertake their duties.
requirements.measurable: A documented mapping of each privileged role to the duties requiring it, plus role/permission dumps and policy tests showing no privileged principal exceeds that mapping.
requirements.why: The general least-privilege clause and the single most valuable ML3 requirement for a codebase to target — it maps almost one-to-one onto artefacts a generator can ship by default.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: Deny-by-default RLS with per-role policies rather than blanket grants; purpose-scoped Postgres roles with minimal GRANTs instead of the owner role; a build-time bundle scan asserting the service_role key never appears behind NEXT_PUBLIC_ or EXPO_PUBLIC_; per-workflow GitHub Actions permissions blocks linted to minimum; OIDC trust policies scoped to a single repo, branch and environment; plus negative-authorization tests asserting each role is denied what it should not hold.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding those explicitly authorised to access online services) are prevented from accessing the internet, email and web services.
requirements.measurable: Technical controls, not policy alone, demonstrably block internet, email and web access from privileged accounts; evidence is proxy/firewall or conditional-access configuration plus a test proving the block.
requirements.why: Privileged credentials are never usable from an internet-exposed surface: service_role key and DB password excluded from the Next.js bundle and Expo binary (build-time secret scan plus a lint rule banning privileged secrets behind public env prefixes), and Supabase network restrictions confining the privileged Postgres role to application and CI egress ranges.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Egress blocking for privileged accounts on the corporate network and endpoint fleet — the literal control.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts explicitly authorised to access online services are strictly limited to only what is required for users and services to undertake their duties.
requirements.measurable: For each privileged account permitted online access, an enumerated allow-list of the specific services and scopes it may reach, with configuration evidence that access beyond the list is blocked.
requirements.why: Privileged CI and service identities must reach the internet, which is exactly the 'explicitly authorised' carve-out; each is scope-minimised — fine-grained GitHub PATs bound to one repository, OIDC trust policies restricted to one repo/branch/environment, Vercel tokens scoped to one project, Supabase keys constrained by RLS. The scope configuration is checked in and diffable.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Scope decisions for human privileged accounts in platform consoles.

requirements.text: Secure Admin Workstations are used in the performance of administrative activities.
requirements.measurable: Administrative activities performed only from a hardened, minimised-attack-surface environment; evidence is the SAW build/hardening configuration plus logs showing admin sessions originating only from SAWs. ASD's FAQ states a SAW is a philosophy of minimising the privileged environment's attack surface, not an equipment specification, and dedicated physical workstations are not required.
requirements.why: No human holds production write credentials: migrations and production deploys execute only on an ephemeral CI runner inside a protected GitHub environment with required reviewers, direct psql to production is disabled by network restrictions, and the runner is destroyed after each job. FLAGGED AS ARGUABLE — a strict assessor could reasonably call this org-only.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The hardened endpoint from which a human performs any administration CI cannot — console-only operations, break-glass access.

requirements.text: Privileged users use separate privileged and unprivileged operating environments.
requirements.measurable: Demonstrable separation between the environment used for administrative work and that used for email and web browsing, with evidence privileged credentials are never entered in the unprivileged environment.
requirements.why: Environment separation in topology and trust boundaries: production in a distinct Supabase project and Vercel environment from preview/development with disjoint credentials, and administrative code paths separated from user-facing ones by the server-only boundary and a distinct admin router. Checkable via per-environment variable inventories and router-level authorization tests.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The privileged versus unprivileged desktop environments used by human administrators.

requirements.text: Privileged operating environments are not virtualised within unprivileged operating environments.
requirements.measurable: Architecture evidence that no privileged environment runs as a guest on an unprivileged host; a privileged VM on a user's internet-connected workstation fails.
requirements.why: The intent — the high-trust environment must not sit inside and depend on the low-trust one — maps cleanly: production is a separate Supabase project, not a branch nested under a development project; production secrets are not derivable from preview variables; preview deployments cannot reach the production database.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Hypervisor topology of any privileged environment the organisation runs.

requirements.text: Unprivileged user accounts cannot logon to privileged operating environments.
requirements.measurable: Logon rights configuration denying unprivileged accounts access to privileged environments, plus a negative test showing the attempt is refused.
requirements.why: Deny-by-default authorization at the data and delivery layers: RLS policies and admin procedures reject any principal without the admin role server-side, never trusting a client-side role claim; and fork-PR workflows cannot access production environment secrets (environment protection rules, no pull_request_target with checkout of untrusted refs). Provable with negative-authorization tests.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: OS logon rights on privileged hosts.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding local administrator accounts) cannot logon to unprivileged operating environments.
requirements.measurable: Logon rights configuration denying privileged accounts access to unprivileged environments (local administrator accounts exempted), plus a negative test.
requirements.why: The reverse-direction credential barrier: each environment issues its own Supabase keys and JWT signing secret so a production service_role key is not accepted by preview or development, and the public edge rejects privileged keys presented from a browser or mobile client. A CI check asserting production secret names are absent from preview/development configuration makes it machine-checkable.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: OS logon rights on unprivileged hosts.

requirements.text: Just-in-time administration is used for administering systems and applications.
requirements.measurable: Privileged access granted only for the duration of the task and automatically revoked; evidence is elevation records with start and end timestamps showing accounts are unprivileged at rest.
requirements.why: Literally implementable in both the pipeline and the application rather than merely analogous.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: GitHub OIDC-issued short-lived credentials (minutes) for each deploy or migration job instead of a long-lived PAT, visible in the workflow YAML and token TTL configuration; plus an admin_sessions table carrying expires_at with the RLS admin predicate requiring now() < expires_at, so accounts are unprivileged at rest and the elevation rows are the evidence.

requirements.text: Administrative activities are conducted through jump servers.
requirements.measurable: Network and access-control evidence that administrative connections originate only from designated jump servers, corroborated by jump server session logs.
requirements.why: A single audited choke point: Supabase network restrictions permit database connections only from application and CI egress ranges so no engineer connects from a laptop, and privileged data operations are exposed exclusively through audited admin procedures or CI workflows, both logging every invocation. The CI runner plus the admin procedure layer play the bastion's role in a topology with no bastion host.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Administration of any organisation-operated infrastructure outside this stack.

requirements.text: Credentials for break glass accounts, local administrator accounts and service accounts are long, unique, unpredictable and managed.
requirements.measurable: Credentials at least 30 characters (the number is from ASD's FAQ; the model text says only 'long'), randomly generated, unique per account, held in a managed secret store, and rotated; evidence is secret-store configuration, rotation records and a repository scan showing no credential is committed.
requirements.why: Every noun has a literal referent: the break glass account is the Supabase/Vercel organisation owner login; the service accounts are the service_role key, database password, CI deploy tokens and the Expo EAS token.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A gitleaks step in CI failing the build on any committed credential; a committed secret inventory with a length/entropy assertion run against it; and Vercel/GitHub encrypted secret store configuration with a recorded rotation schedule rather than credentials in files.

requirements.text: Memory integrity functionality is enabled.
requirements.measurable: Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity (HVCI) reported as enabled and running across in-scope Windows workstations and servers.
requirements.why: A Windows kernel feature toggled via Group Policy, Intune or the registry. Nothing in the repo, its CI, or the deployed application can enable or evidence it; there is no defensible analogue and claiming one would be fabrication.

requirements.text: Local Security Authority protection functionality is enabled.
requirements.measurable: LSA protection (Process Protection Light for LSASS) reported as enabled and running across in-scope Windows hosts. Note the model says 'Local Security Authority' while the FAQ says 'Local System Authority' — same Microsoft control; the FAQ wording appears to be the error.
requirements.why: Protects LSASS against credential dumping. There is no LSASS here, no Windows hosts administered, and no configuration surface. Mapping it to 'protect secrets in process memory' would be hand-waving.

requirements.text: Credential Guard functionality is enabled.
requirements.measurable: Windows Defender Credential Guard reported as configured and running (virtualisation-based security active) on in-scope Windows workstations and servers.
requirements.why: Uses Windows VBS to isolate NTLM and Kerberos secrets, defeating pass-the-hash. It exists only on Windows hosts and depends on endpoint hardware and GPO/Intune; there is no equivalent in a Supabase/JWT model that would honestly stand in.

requirements.text: Remote Credential Guard functionality is enabled.
requirements.measurable: Remote Credential Guard configured for Remote Desktop so credentials are not delegated to the remote host; evidence is GPO/registry settings on both client and target plus connection logs.
requirements.why: Presupposes RDP, Windows clients and Windows targets under the organisation's control. This stack has no RDP and no Windows administration path.

requirements.text: Privileged access events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: A central log store containing privileged access events (who, what, when, from where) across all in-scope systems, applications and data repositories, with demonstrated coverage rather than sampling.
requirements.why: The application can do this literally, and coverage is machine-checkable rather than sampled — absence of logging fails CI rather than surfacing at assessment.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A Postgres AFTER trigger writing an append-only audit row for every action performed under the admin role; a committed log-drain config shipping Supabase Auth, Postgres and Vercel function logs plus the GitHub organisation audit log to one sink; and integration tests asserting each admin mutation produces exactly one audit row.

requirements.text: Privileged user account and security group management events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: Central logs containing creation, modification, deletion, enabling and disabling of privileged accounts and all security group membership changes, with actor and timestamp.
requirements.why: The analogue of a security group is the app's role table, and capturing every change to it is directly implementable and assertable.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: An AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE trigger on user_roles (or profiles.role) writing actor, target, old value, new value and timestamp to the central audit log, with a test asserting no grant or revocation can occur without producing a row; plus scheduled ingestion of GitHub org membership/team change events and Supabase project member changes into the same sink.

requirements.text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.measurable: Technical controls prevent alteration or deletion of stored logs by anyone including administrators — append-only storage, write-once retention, or an independent segregated log store — demonstrated by an attempted-modification test.
requirements.why: Same canonical treatment as MFA-16. One artefact satisfies this clause across all four strategies it appears in and must be counted once.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The same append-only audit table migration, the negative CI test asserting UPDATE and DELETE both fail as every role including service_role, and the retention-locked external sink.

requirements.text: Event logs from internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Evidence that internet-facing logs are actually reviewed or alerted on — detection rules, alert history and triage records — not merely collected.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — DOWNGRADED from the source's 'direct' to match identical text under Application control and MFA. Rules are code (authorization-denial spikes, unexpected admin role assumption, service_role use from an unexpected source); the analysis is staffed and ASD's evidence method is a discussion with SOC analysts.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Human triage and its records.

requirements.text: Event logs from non-internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Detection rules and triage records covering internal server logs with the same timeliness as internet-facing systems.
requirements.why: CANONICAL. Once network restrictions are enabled the managed Postgres instance is genuinely the non-internet-facing server here; its pgaudit and Postgres logs are drained and alerted on with committed rules.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Any internal server estate the organisation runs; human triage.

requirements.text: Event logs from workstations are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Endpoint logs or EDR telemetry from the workstation fleet centrally collected and actively analysed, with detection rules and triage records.
requirements.why: CANONICAL. Workstations in ASD's FAQ are every device using a desktop operating system — the endpoint fleet, not the build environment. Pointing at CI runner logs does not hold: a runner is the administrative environment already claimed at RAP-08.

requirements.text: Cyber security events are analysed in a timely manner to identify cyber security incidents.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: A documented triage process with evidence of execution — event queue, triage decisions, and events promoted to incidents with elapsed time from detection.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — DOWNGRADED from the source's 'analogue'. The judgement step is performed by people; the alert rules and severity thresholds feeding it are already claimed at RAP-23/24.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to the chief information security officer, or one of their delegates, as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Incident records showing notification to the CISO or a named delegate, with elapsed time between discovery and notification.
requirements.why: An organisational reporting obligation between people. Holding the runbook naming who to contact does not satisfy it; only the act of reporting does, evidenced in incident management records.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to ASD as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Records of reports lodged with ASD (ReportCyber or the ASD hotline), including reference numbers and elapsed time from discovery to report.
requirements.why: External regulatory notification performed by the organisation; the evidence — an ASD report reference number — exists entirely outside the technical estate.

requirements.text: Following the identification of a cyber security incident, the cyber security incident response plan is enacted.
requirements.measurable: An incident response plan exists and post-incident records demonstrate it was followed — roles activated, steps executed, decisions logged — for actual incidents rather than only exercises.
requirements.why: CANONICAL. Enactment spans containment decisions, communications, legal and executive involvement. A repository should hold the technical runbooks the plan invokes, but possessing runbooks is not enactment.

requirements.text: Application control is implemented on workstations.
requirements.measurable: Assessor checks whether an application control solution (WDAC, AppLocker or third-party) is implemented on workstations. Best evidence per ASD is simulated activity — attempting to run benign test executables — not policy documentation. NOTE: WDAC is not itself a requirement at any maturity level; the model is vendor-neutral.
requirements.why: 'Workstations' means staff and developer endpoint devices managed by the organisation. No repository, CI pipeline or deployed application controls what executes on an employee's laptop; this is an MDM concern.

requirements.text: Application control is implemented on internet-facing servers.
requirements.measurable: Assessor checks whether an application control solution is implemented on internet-facing servers, ideally by attempting to execute a benign unapproved binary and confirming it is blocked.
requirements.why: The executable surface of the internet-facing runtime is exactly one immutable CI-produced artefact: deploys only from CI (no vercel deploy from a laptop), pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, an ESLint no-restricted-globals/no-restricted-imports rule banning eval, new Function, child_process and non-literal dynamic import() in server code, and a CSP with nonce/hash script-src and no unsafe-eval or unsafe-inline.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: OS-level execution control on the managed host, implementable only by the platform provider.

requirements.text: Application control is implemented on non-internet-facing servers.
requirements.measurable: Assessor checks whether an application control solution is implemented on non-internet-facing servers — internal application, database and management servers.
requirements.why: Supply-chain control over what the build and background tier may execute: third-party Actions pinned to full commit SHAs rather than mutable tags, base images pinned by digest, ignore-scripts=true (or an explicit allowlist) so npm lifecycle scripts cannot run arbitrary code at install, and no curl-pipe-bash or ad-hoc npx remote steps in workflow files — all lintable in CI.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Any internal server estate the organisation runs.

requirements.text: Application control is applied to user profiles and temporary folders used by operating systems, web browsers and email clients.
requirements.measurable: Assessor attempts to run benign executables, scripts, DLLs, MSIs, .chm, .hta and .cpl files placed in user profile and temp directories and confirms each is blocked; ASD names E8MVT and the Application Control Verification Tool.
requirements.why: The hazard — code executing from attacker-writable locations — is genuinely present: expo-updates downloads a JS bundle into the app's writable data directory and executes it, so the analogue is expo-updates code signing with a pinned channel so only organisation-signed bundles execute. Second half: nothing written to a Function's /tmp or fetched from an upload bucket is ever required, imported, spawned, or served with an executable/HTML content type, enforced by Content-Disposition: attachment and a non-HTML content type on upload buckets. This is the one place a mobile app really does have the hazard the requirement describes.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: OS user profile and temp folder execution control on endpoints.

requirements.text: Application control is applied to all locations other than user profiles and temporary folders used by operating systems, web browsers and email clients.
requirements.measurable: Same test method applied to every other disk location; for path-based implementations, review of effective access permissions on all allowed paths confirming standard users cannot write to any allowed-to-execute directory.
requirements.why: The deployed filesystem is immutable and read-only apart from /tmp, so no location is simultaneously writable and executable — a property Vercel serverless and Deno Deploy provide by construction, assertable with a smoke test that a write outside /tmp fails. Repo-side, the entire executable set is the reproducible build output plus the lockfile-pinned closure, with no post-deploy code mutation path.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: All other disk locations on endpoints and organisation-operated servers.

requirements.text: Application control restricts the execution of executables, software libraries, scripts, installers, compiled HTML, HTML applications and control panel applets to an organisation-approved set.
requirements.measurable: ASD states the only truly effective check is testing: attempting to execute benign samples of each of the seven file types from writable locations. Free tooling: E8MVT, ASD's Application Control Verification Tool, AirLock Digital's Application Allowlisting Assessment Tool. ASD warns many solutions silently fail to cover .chm, .hta and .cpl.
requirements.why: The most transferable row: 'software libraries' and 'scripts' map onto a JS/TS monorepo. Approved library set = pnpm-lock.yaml with integrity hashes installed --frozen-lockfile from an approved registry, lifecycle scripts disabled, additions gated by Renovate/Dependabot plus CODEOWNERS on the lockfile. Approved browser script set = CSP script-src with nonces or hashes, no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval. CAVEAT an assessor will press: ASD permits only cryptographic hash, publisher certificate (publisher AND product name) and path rules; file and package names are explicitly NOT acceptable, which is a real weakness in the lockfile analogue.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Execution control over the seven named Windows file types on endpoints and servers.

requirements.text: Application control restricts the execution of drivers to an organisation-approved set.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests the rulesets and checks for driver rules. ASD notes AppLocker does not currently support driver control whereas WDAC does.
requirements.why: Drivers are kernel-mode code. Managed serverless runtimes and mobile app sandboxes expose no kernel-code loading surface — the platform forecloses the capability rather than the repo restricting it, so there is no ruleset for a repo to author. The nearest reach, restricting native Node addons, is already claimed at AC-06.

requirements.text: Microsoft’s recommended application blocklist is implemented.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests the rulesets and checks whether Microsoft's recommended application blocklist has been specified. This is a DIFFERENT list from the vulnerable driver blocklist at AC-09; the two are commonly conflated, and older model versions called them 'recommended block rules'.
requirements.why: Both halves of the living-off-the-land mechanism have counterparts: an externally maintained, continuously updated blocklist consumed as a CI gate (GitHub Advisory Database / OSV / pnpm audit failing the build on malicious-package advisories), and a deny-list of the JS runtime's own default-available primitives — eval, new Function, vm, child_process, process.binding, non-literal import() — via ESLint no-restricted-globals/no-restricted-imports.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The Microsoft blocklist itself on Windows endpoints and servers.

requirements.text: Microsoft’s vulnerable driver blocklist is implemented.
requirements.measurable: Assessor checks whether memory integrity has been enabled via the Windows Security app (which automatically enforces the blocklist), or reviews the ruleset for driver rules specifying it. ASD permits AppLocker at ML3 provided this blocklist is enforced via memory integrity.
requirements.why: Satisfied by an OS-level toggle on Windows hosts. There is no kernel-code surface here, and the 'block known-vulnerable versions of trusted components' idea is already claimed at AC-06 and AC-08.

requirements.text: Application control rulesets are validated on an annual or more frequent basis.
requirements.timeframes: Annual or more frequent
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses how rulesets are validated, at what frequency, and the change-management governance. ASD names the observed failure modes: exploitable applications remaining approved, compromised vendor code-signing certificates remaining authorised, and administrator 'get it working' exceptions never removed.
requirements.why: Once the ruleset analogue is fixed (lockfile + CSP script-src + expo-updates signing keys + CI action pins), the cadence is enforceable as code: a scheduled job failing when the allowlist manifest's recorded last-reviewed date is older than 12 months, plus CODEOWNERS review on every lockfile or CSP change. ASD's stale-exception failure mode maps exactly onto expiring eslint-disable comments, @ts-expect-error suppressions and CSP exemptions with a review-by date.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Validation of the actual endpoint application control ruleset.

requirements.text: Allowed and blocked application control events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests screenshots showing BOTH content allowed to execute AND content blocked, then determines whether the logs are centrally stored; logs should ideally record file name, date/time stamp and username. The commonly-missed half is 'allowed' — most implementations log only denials.
requirements.why: Every authorisation decision at the tRPC boundary and every RLS-relevant access emits a structured audit event carrying outcome (allow or deny), actor id, resource and timestamp — matching ASD's file/time/user triple — shipped to one central sink. Browser-side, CSP report-to captures blocked script execution, the literal browser equivalent of a blocked-execution event.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Allowed and blocked execution events from the endpoint application control solution.

requirements.text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether a SIEM, or equivalent, is used to protect event logs from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.why: Same canonical treatment as MFA-16 and RAP-22. One artefact, counted once.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The append-only audit table migration (RLS INSERT/SELECT only; REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE from all roles including service_role; trigger raising on mutation), the committed negative test asserting UPDATE and DELETE both fail, and the one-way drain to an object-lock/WORM sink.

requirements.text: Event logs from internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise; ASD does not quantify 'timely'.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-17.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Human triage and its records.

requirements.text: Event logs from non-internet-facing servers are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor non-internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-18.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Any internal server estate; human triage.
