requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor workstation event logs for signs of compromise.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-19.

requirements.text: Cyber security events are analysed in a timely manner to identify cyber security incidents.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses how SOC analysts analyse events to determine whether an incident occurred; the incident register may also evidence it.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-20.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to the chief information security officer, or one of their delegates, as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to the CISO or delegate and whether typical timeframes are reasonable.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-21.

requirements.text: Cyber security incidents are reported to ASD as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered.
requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to ASD and whether timeframes are reasonable; evidence is ASD report references in the incident register.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-22.

requirements.text: Following the identification of a cyber security incident, the cyber security incident response plan is enacted.
requirements.measurable: Assessor requests the incident response plan for the system and discusses the extent to which it is followed after an incident.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-23.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros are disabled for users that do not have a demonstrated business requirement.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'VBA Macro Notification Settings' enabled and set to 'Disable all macros without notification' for unapproved users, plus Trust Center screenshots, documentation of each user's demonstrated business requirement and approver, the proportion of the user base approved, and evidence permission is revoked when the requirement lapses.
requirements.why: Per-user entitlement to a desktop application feature across a managed Windows fleet plus an organisational approval register. The stack has no users of Microsoft Office; the nearest repo idea (approved-business-need gating of admin capability) is already claimed at RAP-01.

requirements.text: Only Microsoft Office macros running from within a sandboxed environment, a Trusted Location or that are digitally signed by a trusted publisher are allowed to execute.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows the notification setting at 'Disable all macros without notification' (Trusted Locations) or 'Disable all macros except digitally signed macros' (signing); if only signing is used, 'Disable all trusted locations' is checked; each Trusted Location is enumerated and none sits inside a user profile. NOTE the requirement is a three-way disjunction — sandboxing is a first-class option and is usually dropped in paraphrase.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The proposed analogue (expo-updates code signing, frozen lockfile, CSP script-src 'self' with nonces, CI-only Edge Function deploys) is exactly the evidence already claimed at AC-02, AC-04 and AC-06. Counting it again would inflate coverage by double-counting one artefact across two strategies.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros are checked to ensure they are free of malicious code before being digitally signed or placed within Trusted Locations.
requirements.measurable: A documented macro assessment process; assessors demonstrably independent of macro developers; per-macro assessment records and sign-offs dated prior to signing or placement. NOTE introduced November 2023 — the August 2023 Assessment Process Guide had no method; re-derive from the October 2024 guide.
requirements.why: Unique and non-duplicative: code is proven clean before it is signed and published. A release-tag pipeline that must pass SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep), secret scanning, dependency audit and licence checks BEFORE the signing/publish step, with the signing job gated on those outcomes, plus CODEOWNERS-enforced review by someone other than the author — ASD's independence-of-assessor requirement maps exactly onto 'author cannot approve own PR'.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Assessment of actual Office macros before signing.

requirements.text: Only privileged users responsible for checking that Microsoft Office macros are free of malicious code can write to and modify content within Trusted Locations.
requirements.measurable: For each Trusted Location the assessor reviews effective file system permissions directly (preferred over screenshots) and counts the users in groups holding write/modify permission, confirming that set equals the designated macro assessors.
requirements.why: Unique and non-duplicative: write access to the trusted publication surface is restricted to designated reviewers — branch protection on main/release (no direct pushes, required reviews, no force-push), CODEOWNERS gating deploy and migration directories, the artefact registry and Expo code-signing key in an environment with a restricted reviewer list, and the production service-role key issued only to the deploy job. ASD's count-the-principals evidence is reproducible from GitHub access listings.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: File system permissions on actual Trusted Locations.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros digitally signed by an untrusted publisher cannot be enabled via the Message Bar or Backstage View.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Disable all Trust Bar notifications for security issues' enabled AND 'Disable commands' enabled with command bar ID 19092. ASD notes removing the Backstage View option needs this undocumented GUI setting, so this row is frequently only half-implemented.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The no-bypass mapping (expo-updates rejecting unverified bundles, no --no-verify, no continue-on-error on signing jobs, HSTS preload) restates artefacts already claimed at AC-02, AC-04 and UAH-05.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros digitally signed by signatures other than V3 signatures cannot be enabled via the Message Bar or Backstage View.
requirements.measurable: Configuration evidence that only V3-format signed macros execute and that a legacy-signed macro presents no enable affordance; best verified by test. NOTE introduced November 2023 — the August 2023 guide has no method.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The source itself called its mapping (JWT alg allowlisting, TLS 1.2+ floor, current-format attestation bundles) the weakest of the eleven and an intent-level rather than form-level match to a control about a specific Microsoft signature format.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office’s list of trusted publishers is validated on an annual or more frequent basis.
requirements.timeframes: Annual or more frequent basis
requirements.measurable: Assessor enumerates Trust Center > Trusted Publishers; ideally only the organisation's own code-signing certificate appears. Where third-party certificates are listed, dated records of at least annual review plus the mechanism for detecting a certificate needing removal due to compromise or revocation. ASD prefers the organisation re-sign trusted macros with its own certificate.
requirements.why: Unique, non-duplicative, and the timeframe transfers unchanged: a dated, committed trust inventory covering the Expo code-signing certificate and its rotation date, OIDC trust relationships from Actions to Vercel/Supabase, allowlisted registries and scoped tokens, and the Supabase JWT signing keys — enforced by a scheduled CI job failing when the recorded review date is older than twelve months or a certificate is inside its rotation window.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The actual Office trusted publishers list.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros in files originating from the internet are blocked.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Block macros from running in Office files from the Internet' enabled per application. Where unconfigured, internet-sourced macros are blocked by default only in recent Office versions, so version evidence matters. Best verified by opening a Mark-of-the-Web tagged macro-enabled file.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The untrusted-origin mapping (CSP script-src 'self' with nonces, object-src 'none', uploads on a separate origin with Content-Disposition: attachment and nosniff, no dangerouslySetInnerHTML over user content) is the same evidence claimed at AC-04, UAH-07 and UAH-09.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macro antivirus scanning is enabled.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Macro Runtime Scan Scope' enabled with value 1 (MoTW files, the default) or 2 (all files, ASD's ideal); value 0 fails. Alternatively an EICAR-containing macro is detected when run. Requires an AMSI-integrated antivirus product.
requirements.why: There is no AMSI-integrated VBA runtime here. Upload scanning (a Storage webhook submitting objects to ClamAV or a scanning API before they become readable) is a worthwhile control but is not this requirement and has no ASD evidence path in this context.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macros are blocked from making Win32 API calls.
requirements.measurable: Evidence the Defender ASR rule 'Block Win32 API calls from Office macros' is enabled in block mode, not audit mode; E8MVT includes a test file that must be blocked. The rule constrains the macro's Win32 API access, not the VBA language.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The host-primitive denial mapping (no child_process, no node-ffi, Deno explicit permissions, no raw SQL execution) is the same evidence claimed at UAH-06 and AC-02. This is also the ONLY requirement ML2 adds over ML1 for this strategy — the smallest ML1→ML2 delta in the framework.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office macro security settings cannot be changed by users.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'VBA Macro Notification Settings' enabled, greying out the Trust Center control, corroborated by a screenshot showing it is not user-modifiable. ASD's guidance is that macro security controls should be applied via Group Policy for exactly this reason.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The server-controlled-configuration mapping (headers from middleware, RLS reachable only with the service-role key, server-side feature flags) is the same evidence claimed at UAH-05 and UAH-11.

requirements.text: Internet Explorer 11 is disabled or removed.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Disable Internet Explorer 11 as a standalone browser' enabled, or a Windows Features screenshot showing IE11 absent. ASD also expects an application control block rule on iexplore.exe because standard users can still launch IE11 even on Windows 11 — a hidden dependency on Application control.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. Excluding IE11 from browserslist and serving an unsupported-browser response to MSIE user agents does not remove IE11 from an endpoint and does not reduce the risk the requirement addresses. Note this is an ML1 requirement present at all three levels, not new at ML3 as some summaries claim.

requirements.text: Web browsers do not process Java from the internet.
requirements.measurable: For each browser, visit a page containing Java and confirm it does not execute; review plug-ins for Java. A web content filter blocking internet-based Java is accepted where intranet Java is required. CRITICAL: ASD's FAQ states this does NOT include JavaScript — the single most common misreading of the strategy.
requirements.why: The app never delivers plugin-executed content and forbids it: a CSP response header with object-src 'none', no <applet>/<object>/<embed> in the JSX, and no Java/NPAPI-adjacent asset in the build output. A CI test asserts the CSP header on a live preview and greps the bundle for those tags.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Java plug-in state in the browsers on staff endpoints.

requirements.text: Web browsers do not process web advertisements from the internet.
requirements.measurable: Evidence an ad blocker extension is installed in each browser, or a content filter blocks advertisements. ASD explicitly states a built-in pop-up blocker does NOT meet the intent.
requirements.why: The app serves no third-party ad or ad-tech code: no ad SDK in package.json or the Expo dependency tree, and a CSP script-src/connect-src/frame-src allowlist naming only first-party and approved origins so an ad network cannot load even if a dependency tries. Evidence is a dependency-allowlist check plus a CSP header assertion.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Ad blocking in the browsers staff use for the rest of the internet.

requirements.text: Web browsers are hardened using ASD and vendor hardening guidance, with the most restrictive guidance taking precedence when conflicts occur.
requirements.measurable: Hardening delivered via vendor group policy templates and visible in RSoP; ASD points to Microsoft Security Baselines for Edge and Google's Chrome Browser Enterprise Security Configuration Guide. Note 'ASD AND vendor' replaced 'ASD OR vendor' in November 2023 — both must be implemented, most restrictive winning.
requirements.why: The app hardens the browser context it controls via response headers in next.config.js or middleware: Content-Security-Policy (with frame-ancestors), Strict-Transport-Security with preload, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP/COEP/CORP. Evidence is a header-assertion test against a deployed preview URL.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: GPO-delivered browser baselines on the endpoint fleet.

requirements.text: Web browser security settings cannot be changed by users.
requirements.measurable: Inspect each browser for managed indicators — greyed-out controls (Firefox), 'managed by your organisation' (Edge), 'managed by your administrator' (Chrome). Also confirm Java Control Panel settings cannot be user-changed.
requirements.why: Server-side rather than client-side enforcement: CSP delivered as an HTTP header rather than a <meta> tag so page script cannot relax it; session cookies set HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite by the server; authorization enforced by Postgres RLS so a tampered client, edited local storage or flipped flag cannot change what a user may read. Evidence is the RLS migrations plus a test authenticating as a low-privilege user and proving denial.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Browser setting lockdown on endpoints.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office is blocked from creating child processes.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows ASR rules D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A and 26190899-1602-49E8-8B27-EB1D0A1CE869 set to 1; E8MVT ships macro test files exercising each rule.
requirements.why: The underlying rule — a document-handling application must never become a launcher for arbitrary code — maps onto server code processing user uploads: a hard ban on subprocess spawning in request-handling paths via an ESLint no-restricted-imports rule forbidding node:child_process in route handlers, server actions and Edge Functions (Deno additionally requires --allow-run, which is simply not granted).
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The ASR rule on Windows endpoints — Microsoft Office is not in this stack.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office is blocked from creating executable content.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows ASR rules 3B576869-A4EC-4529-8536-B80A7769E899 and BE9BA2D9-53EA-4CDC-84E5-9B1EEEE46550 set to 1; corroborated by E8MVT test files.
requirements.why: User content can never be written where it will later be served or executed as active content: upload buckets private with RLS, objects served with a server-pinned Content-Type and Content-Disposition: attachment (never the client-declared MIME type), SVG and HTML never rendered inline, nothing user-supplied written into public/ or the build output. Evidence is the storage policy migrations plus a test uploading an HTML/SVG payload and asserting the download headers.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The ASR rule on Windows endpoints.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office is blocked from injecting code into other processes.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows ASR rule 75668C1F-73B5-4CF0-BB93-3ECF5CB7CC84 set to 1; corroborated by an E8MVT test file.
requirements.why: Cross-process injection maps onto one user's stored content executing in another user's browser or the server context: a ban on dangerouslySetInnerHTML and eval/new Function over user-derived values, sanitisation of rendered rich text, parameterised queries only (no concatenated SQL; SECURITY DEFINER functions with a pinned search_path), and per-tenant RLS isolation. Evidence is the lint rules, migration review and a stored-XSS regression test.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The ASR rule on Windows endpoints.

requirements.text: Microsoft Office is configured to prevent activation of Object Linking and Embedding packages.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows the 'PackagerPrompt' registry value under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\<application>\Security\ set to REG_DWORD 2; E8MVT can confirm.
requirements.why: OLE is how a passive document activates an embedded foreign object. Embedded objects can never be activated from app-hosted content: CSP object-src 'none', third-party or user-supplied embeds rendered only inside an <iframe sandbox> with a minimal allow-list, and frame-ancestors 'none' against clickjacking. Evidence is a CSP header assertion and a grep for un-sandboxed iframes.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The Office registry setting on Windows endpoints.

requirements.text: Office productivity suites are hardened using ASD and vendor hardening guidance, with the most restrictive guidance taking precedence when conflicts occur.
requirements.measurable: Hardening applied via group policy templates and visible in RSoP; ASD directs assessors to its 'Hardening Microsoft 365, Office 2021, Office 2019 and Office 2016' publication and Microsoft's Security Baselines Blog, more restrictive winning on conflict.
requirements.why: The generalised control — every platform the app is built on is configured per its vendor's published guidance, strictest wins — is concrete: Supabase security advisors run clean (RLS on every public table, no SECURITY DEFINER views, leaked-password protection on, pinned function search_path), Next.js per its production security checklist, Expo per its app-security guidance. Evidence is a CI step failing the build on any outstanding Supabase security advisor finding.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Hardening of the actual Office productivity suite on endpoints.

requirements.text: Office productivity suite security settings cannot be changed by users.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows security-related group policy settings defined for Microsoft Office, or screenshots of each application's security settings greyed out.
requirements.why: Security configuration is declared in version-controlled infrastructure rather than runtime-mutable: RLS policies, grants and auth settings exist only as migrations under supabase/migrations, applied by CI, with production write access held by no interactive human account. A drift check (supabase db diff against the migration set, failing on any difference) is the machine-checkable evidence that nothing changed out of band.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Office setting lockdown on endpoints.

requirements.text: PDF software is blocked from creating child processes.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows ASR rule 7674BA52-37EB-4A4F-A9A1-F0F9A1619A2C set to 1. ASD notes it applies only to Adobe PDF software and suggests a manual test: from Acrobat use File-Open, show all files, right-click an .exe and select Open — the rule should block it.
requirements.why: Same mechanism as UAH-06 scoped to the document-rendering path: PDFs rendered client-side in a sandboxed context (pdf.js in a Web Worker inside an <iframe sandbox>, or the mobile OS document viewer), and any server-side PDF handling using an in-process library rather than shelling out to pdftoppm or ghostscript. Evidence is the absence of exec/spawn in the document pipeline, enforced by lint.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The ASR rule on endpoints running Adobe Acrobat.

requirements.text: PDF software is hardened using ASD and vendor hardening guidance, with the most restrictive guidance taking precedence when conflicts occur.
requirements.measurable: Hardening typically applied via registry settings and visible in RSoP; ASD directs assessors to Adobe's 'Security Configuration Guide for Acrobat'.
requirements.why: The PDF library the app ships is itself hardened and current: pdf.js instantiated with isEvalSupported: false and enableScripting: false so embedded PDF JavaScript cannot run, version pinned in the lockfile, and audit/Dependabot gating the build on known CVEs. Evidence is the viewer's option object in source plus a passing audit step.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Hardening of the PDF reader installed on endpoints.

requirements.text: PDF software security settings cannot be changed by users.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows security-related group policy settings for PDF software, or screenshots showing the controls greyed out.
requirements.why: THE WEAKEST ANALOGUE IN THIS REGISTER, flagged rather than dressed up: the UAH-13 hardening flags are compile-time constants in the source bundle with no UI toggle, environment variable or remote-config key an end user or support operator could flip at runtime. Evidence is that a grep for the flag names finds exactly one definition site, in source, and no code path reads them from a user- or config-controlled value.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: PDF reader setting lockdown on endpoints.

requirements.text: .NET Framework 3.5 (includes .NET 2.0 and 3.0) is disabled or removed.
requirements.measurable: Screenshot of Windows Features checking whether '.NET Framework 3.5 (includes .NET 2.0 and .NET 3.0)' shows a tick or black square. ASD notes enabling .NET 3.5 automatically enables PowerShell 2.0, so this and UAH-16 must be assessed together.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The proposed mapping — no EOL runtime or deprecated dependency in the build — is the identical evidence already claimed at PA-11, PA-13 and POS-16. The literal artefact is a Windows optional feature toggle.

requirements.text: Windows PowerShell 2.0 is disabled or removed.
requirements.measurable: Screenshot of Windows Features checking for 'Windows PowerShell 2.0'; ASD supplies Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -online | Where-Object {$_.FeatureName -match "PowerShellv2"} to confirm whether a downgrade is available.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The no-downgrade-path mapping (TLS floor, no legacy auth flow alongside PKCE, minimum-supported-app-version gate) restates controls claimed at MFA-10 and MFA-13. The literal artefact is a Windows optional feature.

requirements.text: PowerShell is configured to use Constrained Language Mode.
requirements.measurable: Screenshot of $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode — 'ConstrainedLanguage' passes, 'FullLanguage' fails. ASD's rationale is that it prevents running tools that exploit PowerShell or load COM objects, libraries and classes into a session.
requirements.why: The STRONGEST analogue in this strategy and retained for that reason: 'the interpreter available to an attacker runs in a restricted language mode'. In the browser the interpreter is JavaScript and the restriction is a CSP with no unsafe-eval and no unsafe-inline (nonce or hash based) plus no eval/new Function/dynamic Function construction in the bundle; server-side the database exposes only parameterised queries and named RPCs and Edge Functions run under a minimal explicit Deno permission set. Evidence: a CI check asserting unsafe-eval is absent from the deployed CSP header and a grep of the built bundle for eval sinks.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: PowerShell language mode on Windows endpoints.

requirements.text: PowerShell module logging, script block logging and transcription events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Turn on Module Logging', 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' and 'Turn on PowerShell Transcription' all enabled, module logging ideally set to '*', and the assessor must confirm central storage rather than local retention.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The requirement names three specific PowerShell logging providers; the generalised 'server-side execution is logged centrally' mapping is a different control whose evidence (log drains from route handlers, Postgres, Auth, Storage and Edge Functions) is already claimed at RAP-20 and AC-11. Note this requirement changed shape in November 2023 — it used to mean application control events for blocked PowerShell scripts.

requirements.text: Command line process creation events are centrally logged.
requirements.measurable: RSoP shows 'Audit Process Creation' enabled with value 'Success' under Detailed Tracking AND 'Include command line in process creation events' enabled, with central storage confirmed. ASD's intent is to cover both shells an actor can use on a compromised device.
requirements.why: RECLASSIFIED from 'analogue'. The subject is OS process creation with command lines on hosts the organisation runs. The control-plane audit mapping (Actions run logs, org audit log, Supabase project audit log, service-role key attribution) is already claimed at RAP-20 and RAP-21.

requirements.text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether a SIEM, or equivalent, protects logs from unauthorised modification and deletion; demonstrated write-once retention is stronger evidence.
requirements.why: Same canonical treatment as MFA-16, RAP-22 and AC-12. One artefact, counted once across all four strategies.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: The append-only audit table migration (RLS INSERT/SELECT only; REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE from every role including service_role; ON UPDATE/ON DELETE rule or trigger raising), the committed negative test asserting both fail as every role, and the log drain to object storage with a retention lock.

requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise; supporting evidence is detection rules plus records of triage.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — DOWNGRADED from the source's 'direct' to match identical text under Application control and MFA. See MFA-17.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Human triage and its records.

requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor non-internet-facing server logs for signs of compromise.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-18.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Any internal server estate; human triage.

requirements.text: Event logs from workstations are analysed in a timely manner to detect cyber security events.
requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses whether SOC analysts monitor workstation event logs for signs of compromise, with central collection rather than local retention.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-19.

requirements.timeframes: in a timely manner (ASD sets no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses how SOC analysts analyse events to determine whether an incident occurred; the incident register may also evidence it.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — DOWNGRADED from the source's 'analogue'. See MFA-20.

requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to the CISO or delegate and whether typical timeframes are reasonable.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-21.

requirements.timeframes: as soon as possible after they occur or are discovered (no numeric window)
requirements.measurable: Assessor discusses reporting to ASD and whether timeframes are reasonable; corroborating evidence is ReportCyber submissions or ASD case references.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-22.

requirements.measurable: Assessor requests the incident response plan and discusses the extent to which it is followed; post-incident reviews are the strongest evidence.
requirements.why: CANONICAL — see MFA-23.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are performed and retained in accordance with business criticality and business continuity requirements.
requirements.timeframes: No fixed numeric window — frequency and retention are set by the organisation's own business criticality and business continuity requirements. ASD deliberately removed the previously prescriptive 'daily' frequency and 'three months or greater' retention; any checklist citing those numbers is pre-2023.
requirements.measurable: ASD directs assessors to discuss backup and retention frequencies including the business criticality of different data sets, and to request the business continuity plan to check frequency and retention are documented. Two-part evidence: a BCP stating the figures, plus backup configuration and job history showing they are met.
requirements.why: DOWNGRADED from 'direct'. The repo holds the whole configuration half — Supabase PITR window and daily-backup retention days, a scheduled pg_dump/storage-sync job, object-store lifecycle rules, and a CI assertion that configuration >= a committed policy file — but the requirement's yardstick is 'in accordance with business criticality and business continuity requirements', and without the organisation's BCP there is nothing to be in accordance WITH. Note 'business criticality' was added in November 2023 and is the only change to this strategy in that release.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The business continuity plan supplying the RPO/RTO and criticality classifications.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are synchronised to enable restoration to a common point in time.
requirements.measurable: Evidence that backup jobs for data, applications and settings are coordinated to a shared restore point. ASD's rationale: data backed up out of sync with associated applications and settings hampers restoration and risks data loss. An assessor looks for a single named/timestamped restore point spanning all three classes, not independently scheduled unaligned jobs.
requirements.why: All three artefact classes exist and can be bound into one record: data = Postgres plus Storage buckets; applications = the built Next.js/Expo artefacts and the commit that produced them; settings = migrations, RLS policies, Edge Function source and config manifests.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: A committed restore-manifest artefact emitted per backup binding the git commit SHA, applied migration version, Storage bucket snapshot id and Postgres PITR timestamp (or physical backup LSN); plus a CI assertion that all four fields in the newest manifest refer to the same wall-clock window and that the manifest's migration version matches the schema_migrations state captured in the dump.

requirements.text: Backups of data, applications and settings are retained in a secure and resilient manner.
requirements.measurable: ASD: 'Check what efforts have been made to ensure that backup processes and procedures are secure and resilient. For example, are backups encrypted and how quickly can they be used to recover from IT equipment failures?' Evidence: encryption at rest and in transit, storage isolated from the production failure domain, and a demonstrated recovery time. This is the bullet most often dropped from third-party ML1 checklists.
requirements.why: Every property is infrastructure the repo declares and CI can assert on a schedule.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: Committed infrastructure config placing backup artefacts in an object store in a separate region and separate cloud account from the production Supabase project, with server-side encryption plus an application-layer envelope key held outside the deploy credential, versioning enabled, and integrity checksums recorded in the restore manifest; plus a scheduled CI job verifying the checksums and asserting the bucket's encryption, region and cross-account policy.

requirements.text: Restoration of data, applications and settings from backups to a common point in time is tested as part of disaster recovery exercises.
requirements.timeframes: The model text sets no interval; ASD's assessment process guide qualifies it as 'regular (at least annually) disaster recovery exercises', so at least annually is the assessor's working expectation.
requirements.measurable: ASD: discuss whether DR exercises have been conducted, how often, when the last one was, and whether partial or full restoration (data, applications AND settings) was exercised; ideally an after-action review or post-exercise report exists. CRITICAL: 'business-as-usual recovery of user files is not sufficient. Rather, the intent of this control is the restoration of a significant component of a system as part of a scheduled exercise.'
requirements.why: DOWNGRADED from 'direct', which the source itself qualified. A scheduled workflow restoring the newest manifest into a throwaway Supabase project, replaying migrations to the manifest's version, deploying the manifest's commit and running an E2E smoke suite with a dated pass/fail artefact is superb evidence — stronger than the interview method ASD describes — but ASD's subject is an EXERCISE, an organisational activity with participants and an after-action review, and a green CI job is not that.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: The scheduled organisational disaster recovery exercise, its participants, and the after-action review the assessor asks for.

requirements.text: Unprivileged user accounts cannot access backups belonging to other user accounts.
requirements.measurable: ASD: review the backup solution and AD security groups to determine who has access; where backups are on network shares, request a demonstration of effective access permissions showing an unprivileged account cannot access backups beyond their own. Evidence is an effective-permissions demonstration, not a policy statement.
requirements.why: The literal control is NTFS/AD permissions on a backup share. Mapping: the unprivileged identity is the Postgres anon and authenticated role reached through PostgREST — REVOKE ALL on the backup schema, default-deny RLS with no permissive SELECT policy, per-user export buckets private with RLS keyed on auth.uid(), signed URLs per-object and short-lived. Testable with pgTAP/RLS tests asserting user A gets zero rows and 403s for user B's objects, plus a grant-audit query.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Backup-share permissions for any organisation-operated backup solution outside this stack.

requirements.text: Unprivileged user accounts cannot access their own backups.
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 guidance but apply the more restrictive access control — unprivileged accounts should no longer be able to access their OWN backups. At ML1 and ML2 self-access was explicitly acceptable ('it is not necessarily a problem if they are able to access their own backups'), so the assessor is checking for the tightening.
requirements.why: Same identity mapping as RB-05 with the self-access carve-out removed: anon and authenticated have no read path to ANY backup artefact including their own — no self-service 'download my backup' route, no signed-URL issuance for the backup bucket from any user-facing procedure, REVOKE SELECT on all backup/snapshot tables from authenticated, default-deny RLS on the backup bucket's storage.objects rows. DESIGN TENSION WORTH FLAGGING: a GDPR/Privacy Act data-export feature is NOT a backup and must be built from live tables, not from the backup artefact, or this control breaks.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Backup-share permissions outside this stack.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) cannot access backups belonging to other user accounts.
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 guidance with more restrictive access control — privileged accounts should only be able to access their own backups, except backup administrator accounts. Assessors are pointed at AD queries and tools such as BloodHound to enumerate which accounts are privileged and which are genuinely backup administrators.
requirements.why: Privileged identities here are the service_role key, the CI deploy identity, and human developers with Supabase or Vercel dashboard access. Define one narrow backup-administrator principal (a dedicated IAM role assumed only by the backup job) and deny every other privileged principal read access — no GetObject on the backup bucket for the deploy role, minimal Supabase org member roles, and a separate project/account boundary so production service_role confers nothing over the backup bucket. Checkable by asserting each non-backup principal's effective policy contains no read action on the backup bucket ARN.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Domain-admin-class account permissions on any organisation-operated backup solution.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) cannot access their own backups.
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 guidance with more restrictive access control — privileged accounts (excluding backup administrators) should no longer be able to access their own backups. The delta being assessed is removal of the self-access carve-out ML2 permitted.
requirements.why: Same mapping as RB-07 with self-access removed: the deploy role, service_role and developer identities get zero read access to the backup store including any backup of their own environment, because the backup bucket's resource policy allows only the dedicated backup-administrator principal and explicitly Denies all others, so an admin cannot self-grant via an identity policy. Checkable by an IAM policy-simulator assertion in CI that each non-backup principal is denied GetObject/ListBucket.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Privileged account permissions on any organisation-operated backup solution.

requirements.text: Unprivileged user accounts are prevented from modifying and deleting backups.
requirements.measurable: ASD: check whether unprivileged accounts can modify or delete their own backups; where backups are on network shares, demonstrate effective access permissions showing they cannot modify, delete, OR take ownership of content to change permissions. The 'take ownership' clause matters — the assessor checks indirect paths to write access. Note the verb is 'modifying AND deleting'; blocking delete while permitting overwrite fails, since ASD's stated threat is ransomware 'overwriting or deleting backups'.
requirements.why: anon and authenticated hold no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE grants on any backup or snapshot table and no permissive RLS write policy on the backup bucket's storage.objects rows, and no user-session-reachable mutation touches backup artefacts. The 'take ownership' equivalent is privilege-escalation paths — a SECURITY DEFINER function callable by authenticated that writes to backup tables, or an RLS policy whose USING clause a user can influence. Checkable by a pgTAP suite asserting write denial under a real user JWT plus a static check that no SECURITY DEFINER function granted to authenticated references the backup schema.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Write/ownership permissions on any organisation-operated backup share.

requirements.text: Privileged user accounts (excluding backup administrator accounts) are prevented from modifying and deleting backups.
requirements.measurable: ASD: use the ML1 guidance with more restrictive access control — privileged accounts should no longer be able to modify and delete backups; such activities are restricted to backup administrator accounts, provisioned per least privilege and separation of duties (a small group of trusted administrators, with a separate group for restoring).
requirements.why: The CI deploy role, service_role and developer identities are denied PutObject, DeleteObject, DeleteObjectVersion and lifecycle/bucket-policy mutation on the backup bucket; only a dedicated backup-writer role may write and a distinct backup-restore role may only read into a scratch project, reproducing ASD's separation of duties. Checkable by asserting the bucket resource policy and each principal's effective permissions in CI. The residual gap from 'direct' is the cloud provider's root/organisation owner above the policy — which is exactly what RB-11 closes.
requirements.orgOnlyResidue: Privileged account write permissions on any organisation-operated backup solution.

requirements.text: Backup administrator accounts are prevented from modifying and deleting backups during their retention period.
requirements.timeframes: 'during their retention period' — the window is the organisation's own documented retention period set under RB-01, not an ASD-specified number. Deletion is permitted once that period has been exceeded.
requirements.measurable: ASD: backup administrator accounts should no longer be able to modify and delete backups during the retention period, but may do so afterwards; where such activity is required during the period it 'need[s] to be restricted to break glass accounts'. NOTE 'break glass accounts' appears only in the assessment process guide, NOT in the maturity model text — do not cite it as model wording. Evidence: an immutability/retention-lock mechanism whose window matches the documented retention period, a demonstration that a backup administrator's delete attempt fails inside that window, and a controlled, logged break-glass path.
requirements.why: This maps onto WORM object storage exactly rather than by analogy: compliance-mode object lock is enforced by the storage service against every principal INCLUDING the account root and the backup-administrator role, so no identity policy can override it — the exact property ASD describes. Deletion inside the window then genuinely requires a break-glass path, auditable in the provider's audit trail.
requirements.evidenceIfDirect: Committed infrastructure config enabling S3 Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode (or the equivalent immutable-blob policy) on the backup bucket with default retention equal to the documented retention days; a CI assertion that GetObjectLockConfiguration returns COMPLIANCE with retention days >= the value in the committed retention policy file; and a negative test asserting the backup role's DeleteObject on a locked object returns AccessDenied.
